It just triggers more \"what-if\" loops and keeps me from being able to shut my brain off.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that these repetitive checking behaviors are aimed at reducing anxiety in general, or are they specifically focused on preventing a perceived catastrophe or mistake, and do you feel compelled to perform them?\n\nPatient: They are definitely driven by a fear of making mistakes or causing a catastrophe, like a deployment slipping, looking incompetent, or my family suffering. The anxiety just persists and actually escalates because I start worrying about the next thing I might have missed.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like these checking behaviors are excessive or unreasonable, and are they causing significant distress or impairment in your daily life, such as affecting your relationships or work performance?\n\nPatient: Yes, they definitely feel excessive and completely out of control, especially when I'm up late rereading code or constantly obsessing over our budget. The worries aren't limited to just one area; instead, they chain together so that a minor work issue, like a deployment delay, quickly snowballs into worst-case scenarios about my kids getting sick, my parents falling, or my wife resenting me.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself actively trying to avoid certain situations, places, or activities because they trigger or worsen these 'what-if' scenarios and feelings of tension?\n\nPatient: I don't really avoid specific places or situations, because the tension and \"what-if\" thoughts seem to follow me everywhere, even during routine tasks at home or work. Instead of avoiding things, I usually find myself trying to over-prepare or constantly rework my projects to try and manage the anxiety.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself repeating certain behaviors or mental acts, such as checking or counting, in an attempt to reduce your anxiety or prevent perceived disasters?\n\nPatient: I don't do classic physical rituals or counting, but I definitely struggle with repetitive checking behaviors. I constantly check Jira and the family budget in my head, and I spend hours late at night rereading code and project plans over and over to prevent any mistakes. It's like I'm constantly double-checking everything to keep a disaster from happening.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about how these checking behaviors, like re-reading code and project plans, specifically help you feel like you're preventing disasters or reducing your anxiety?\n\nPatient: In the moment, checking Jira or rereading code feels like the only way to gain control and stop a disaster, like a deployment slipping and making me look incompetent. But in reality, it doesn't actually reduce my anxiety. It just triggers more \"what-if\" loops and keeps me from being able to shut my brain off.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that these repetitive checking behaviors are aimed at reducing anxiety in general, or are they specifically focused on preventing a perceived catastrophe or mistake, and do you feel compelled to perform them?\n\nPatient: They are definitely driven by a fear of making mistakes or causing a catastrophe, like a deployment slipping, looking incompetent, or my family suffering. I feel completely compelled to do them because my mind constantly chains those \"what-if\" scenarios that I can't shut off. It feels like I have to keep checking just to prevent everything from falling apart.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if you feel a significant sense of relief or reduction in anxiety immediately after performing these checking behaviors, or if the anxiety persists despite your efforts to check and recheck?\n\nPatient: No, I don't get any relief from checking at all. Instead of calming me down, looking at Jira or reviewing the family budget just triggers a whole new chain of \"what-if\" scenarios. The anxiety just persists and actually escalates because I start worrying about the next thing I might have missed.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like these checking behaviors are excessive or unreasonable, and are they causing significant distress or impairment in your daily life, such as affecting your relationships or work performance?\n\nPatient: Yes, they definitely feel excessive and completely out of control, especially when I'm up late rereading code or constantly obsessing over our budget. It is causing massive strain at home—I've missed family events, snap at my wife constantly, and she says she feels like she's parenting a third child instead of having a partner. It's even affecting my job, as my latest performance reviews actually flag \"focus issues\" because I zone out so much during meetings.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you experience any significant distress or impairment when you're unable to perform these checking behaviors, such as when you're in a meeting or away from your computer?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. Even when I'm away from my computer or in a meeting, I end up doing all that checking \"in my head,\" which keeps me incredibly tense. It triggers those constant \"what-if\" loops, causing me to zone out, lose my train of thought, and completely fail to focus on what is actually happening in front of me.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your repetitive checking behaviors are attempts to neutralize or cope with the obsessive 'what-if' thoughts, or are they more driven by a need for perfection or control in your work and personal life?\n\nPatient: It's really a mix of both. The checking is a desperate attempt to stop those cascading \"what-if\" thoughts, like a slipped deployment making me look incompetent and causing my family to suffer. At the same time, it's driven by an exhausting drive to outperform, where I feel like I'm solely responsible for keeping everything at work and home running perfectly so it doesn't all collapse.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if you have ever experienced a period where your obsessive 'what-if' thoughts and compulsive checking behaviors were significantly reduced or absent, and if so, what triggered that change?\n\nPatient: Honestly, I haven't really experienced a period where these thoughts and behaviors were reduced or absent since this all started nine months ago. On one hand, I’m trying to prevent specific dreaded outcomes, like a deployment slipping, looking incompetent at work, or failing to provide for my family. I feel solely responsible for keeping everything running smoothly, so I constantly worry about specific outcomes like a deployment failing, my parents falling, or my kids suffering. At the same time, my drive to outperform and fear of looking incompetent or failing as a husband and father feed into those endless \"what-if\" loops, keeping me up late rereading code and checking plans.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you believe your repetitive checking behaviors are aimed at preventing a specific, dreaded event from occurring, or if they are more about trying to reduce your overall feelings of anxiety and uncertainty?\n\nPatient: It’s really driven by both. On one hand, I’m trying to prevent specific dreaded outcomes, like a deployment slipping, looking incompetent at work, or failing to provide for my family. But at the same time, it feels like an uncontrollable mental loop where I’m just desperately trying to quiet the constant \"what-if\" scenarios and ease this overwhelming sense of anxiety and uncertainty.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your obsessive 'what-if' thoughts and compulsive checking behaviors are more closely intertwined, with the thoughts driving the behaviors, or do you experience them as somewhat separate, with the thoughts being more about general anxiety and the behaviors being attempts to cope with that anxiety?\n\nPatient: They feel deeply intertwined, with the \"what-if\" thoughts directly driving my need to check. When my mind starts chaining those worst-case scenarios—like a deployment slipping, looking incompetent, or my family suffering—it makes me feel like I have to constantly check Jira, reread code, or review the budget to prevent those disasters. Even though it doesn't actually stop the anxiety, the thoughts make the checking feel absolutely necessary in the moment.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any specific times or situations when your obsessive 'what-if' thoughts and compulsive checking behaviors are notably worse or better, and what factors you think might influence this variation?\n\nPatient: The \"what-if\" thoughts and mental checking get significantly worse when I'm trying to wind down, like when I'm lying in bed at night or trying to play on the floor with my kids. They are mainly triggered by work pressures like sprint reviews and deployments, combined with domestic logistics like daycare pickups and financial planning. Lately, things rarely get better, because any quiet moment just seems to let all that anxiety rush right back in.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your obsessive 'what-if' thoughts and compulsive checking behaviors are primarily focused on preventing a specific type of harm or negative outcome, such as financial ruin or harm to loved ones, which might help distinguish between generalized anxiety and a more specific obsessive-compulsive pattern?\n\nPatient: It’s not focused on just one specific harm, but rather an uncontrollable chain reaction across all areas of my life. For example, a small worry about a work deployment slipping chains into looking incompetent, which leads to financial worries about not being able to move, and eventually to worrying my kids will suffer. I also constantly worry about other distinct things like my kids getting sick, my parents falling, or my wife resenting me, so it's really about everything all at once.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate what percentage of your daily thoughts are consumed by these 'what-if' scenarios and compulsive checking behaviors, and how much of your day is spent actively engaging in these thoughts and behaviors?\n\nPatient: I'd estimate that these thoughts and mental checks consume easily 80% to 90% of my waking hours. It feels like a heavy background process that is constantly running, even when I’m trying to focus on work or be present with my family. I end up spending hours late into the night actively stuck in those \"what-if\" chains—rereading code or mentally reviewing Jira and our budget—because I just can't shut it off.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you experience any ego-dystonic thoughts, meaning thoughts that are unwelcome, intrusive, and go against your values or desires, which might help differentiate between obsessive-compulsive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder?\n\nPatient: I don't think I experience those kinds of thoughts. My worries, while overwhelming and constant, are always about real-life things like my family's well-being, work deadlines, and our finances, rather than thoughts that feel foreign or against my core values. Even when I am actively trying to do other things—like playing on the floor with my kids or sitting on the couch with my wife—I just can't shut the thoughts off. The \"what-ifs\" keep chaining in my head, and I remain too tense and keyed up to actually relax or be present.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if there are any specific, recurrent, and intrusive thoughts or images that you try to suppress or neutralize, which are not just worries about everyday things, but rather thoughts that feel strange or uncharacteristic of you?\n\nPatient: No, I don't have any strange or bizarre thoughts like that at all. My worries are strictly focused on everyday responsibilities, like my work deadlines, our family finances, my kids' health, and my parents. It’s just that these normal concerns feel incredibly overwhelming, blown way out of proportion, and completely impossible to turn off.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you experience any thoughts that are repetitive, intrusive, and specifically focused on a particular theme, such as contamination, harm, or symmetry, which might help differentiate between obsessive-compulsive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder?"

At the same time, my drive to outperform and fear of looking incompetent or failing as a husband and father feed into those endless \"what-if\" loops, keeping me up late rereading code and checking plans.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you believe your repetitive checking behaviors are aimed at preventing a specific, dreaded event from occurring, or if they are more about trying to reduce your overall feelings of anxiety and uncertainty?\n\nPatient: It’s really driven by both. When my mind starts chaining those worst-case scenarios—like a deployment slipping, looking incompetent, or my family suffering—it makes me feel like I have to constantly check Jira, reread code, or review the budget to prevent those disasters. Even though it doesn't actually stop the anxiety, the thoughts make the checking feel absolutely necessary in the moment.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any specific times or situations when your obsessive 'what-if' thoughts and compulsive checking behaviors are notably worse or better, and what factors you think might influence this variation?\n\nPatient: The \"what-if\" thoughts and mental checking get significantly worse when I'm trying to wind down, like when I'm lying in bed at night or trying to play on the floor with my kids. They are mainly triggered by work pressures like sprint reviews and deployments, combined with domestic logistics like daycare pickups and financial planning.
